title: Stacked ledger (bars): where does the total come from?
summary: Bars divided into stacked parts with a line of markers showing each bar's total. The total is visible, the first part is easy to compare, and the later parts need care.

media.alt: Stacked bar chart with five categories, teal lower parts and amber upper parts, and a rose dashed line with dot markers at each bar's total.
media.caption: Reference render with synthetic demonstration data (design-system gallery).

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: Where does the total come from?
read_the_figure.axes: x: categories A to E. y: value (0 to about 3.8, units not stated). Each bar stacks part 1 (teal, bottom) and part 2 (amber, top). Rose dashed line with dots: the total of each bar.
look_at: Does the total marker sit exactly at the top of each stack?
Which bar has the largest total, and which part makes it large?
Which part can you compare across bars accurately (the bottom one)?
What does the dashed line between categories claim?
read_the_figure.proves: The total of each category and its split into two parts, with a direct check: marker on top of stack. It shows composition, but only the bottom part is comparable between bars.
if_wrong: No total line or marker: the reader must add the parts by eye.
A total line that joins unrelated categories: it implies a trend between A and B.
Units missing from the y axis: 'value' is not a quantity.

terms.meaning: A bar split into parts placed one on top of the other; the length is the total.
A record of parts and totals: what comes in, what goes out, and the sum.
The zero line from which a bar segment is measured; only the bottom segment has the common axis as baseline.
A relation in which several parts make one total.
A mark placed at the sum of the parts to check and emphasise the total.

remember: Only the bottom part has a common baseline; compare the top part by its length, not its position.
Marker should land at the top of the stack: it is the check.
Never connect categories with a line unless there is an order.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Bar height encodes the total, the colour of the segments encodes the part, and segment length encodes the part's size. The rose dots mark the total independently of the stack and the dashed line connects them. A legend at the top names the three series. The y axis has gridlines for reading values.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: The question where does the total come from is a part-to-whole question, and the stacked bar answers it directly: the total is the bar, the parts are its pieces. The bottom part is compared by position on a common scale, the most accurate channel. A marker for the total lets the reader see the check that the parts sum to the total.

understand.title: Read this reference render
understand.text: Q1: Which total is largest? B at about 3.8, built from 2.76 (part 1) and 1.04 (part 2). Q2: Which part 2 is largest? A, at about 1.57 (the top of A, 3.02, minus 1.45), then E at about 1.31. Reading the top segment of A (from 1.45 to 3.02) is harder than reading the bottom one because it has no baseline. Q3: Do the total markers match the stacks? Yes: the rose markers sit at 3.0, 3.8, 2.4, 3.5 and 2.5 which are the tops of the stacks, so parts sum to totals; the five totals sum to about 15.2.

understand.title: The must-check list, explained
understand.text: Total line: the marker line is what the figure adds over a plain stack: the sum is stated, not left to be read. Without it a reader would add two segment lengths by eye for each bar, with error.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: Only the bottom segment is aligned; the amber part starts at a different height in each bar, so comparing it between bars means comparing lengths with no baseline, which is a poorer judgement. The dashed line implies a trend or continuity between categories that are separate. Totals and parts have different scales: the part of a small bar looks tiny. A truncated y axis would exaggerate the differences. More than 3 or 4 parts make a stack unreadable.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: A grouped bar chart gives every part a common baseline; a table with totals is exact; a 100 percent stacked bar compares shares; a waterfall shows parts building up to one total; a dot plot of each part against the category.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Replace the dashed line by markers with no line, label each segment with its value, and add a small panel of the shares of part 2 in each category.

steps.title: Part-to-whole identity
steps.note: Share of part 2 in category k.

steps.title: Grand total
steps.note: The sum over categories of the totals equals the sum of the parts: 9.03 + 6.14 = 15.17.

worked.title: Reading the parts of bar A
worked.problem: Bar A: part 1 reaches 1.45, the top of the stack is at 3.02. Find part 2, its share and the grand total from the five totals 3.02, 3.80, 2.37, 3.47, 2.51.
worked.answer: Part 2 is 1.57 (52 percent of A); the five totals sum to 15.17.

analyze.q: Which bar has the largest share of part 2, and how did you decide without reading numbers?
analyze.hint: Compare the amber height to the total height.

analyze.q: What would a connecting line suggest to a reader who sees A to E as places along a pipe?

evaluate.q: Is the stacked form right when the main question is to compare part 2 between categories?
evaluate.hint: Which form gives a common baseline?

create: Redraw as grouped bars with the total as a separate bar and compare which question each form answers.
Add the shares in a 100 percent version beside it.

checks.q: What does the rose marker show?
checks.answer: The total of the two parts for each bar.

checks.q: Part 1 is 2.76 and the total is 3.80. Part 2?
Part 2 is similar in B and C but looks different on the chart. Why?
checks.answer: Part 2 sits at different heights, so no common baseline; the eye compares positions, not lengths, and is misled; use grouped bars or labels.
